activity: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places
knowledge_domain: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places
fact: Protons have a positive charge, electrons have a negative charge, and neutrons have no charge at all.
story:
The gym smelled like glue and popcorn, and the folding tables stretched in rows all the way to the bleachers. Brayden set his shoebox on the table and lifted the lid. Inside, on a tangle of floral wire, hung his model of a lithium atom: a cluster of beads for the nucleus, and three lonely beads orbiting on wire rings. Sara leaned over from the next table, where her volcano waited with its lump of red foam.

"Those middle ones are supposed to be different colours," she said. "Yours are all yellow."

Brayden looked down. He had glued three yellow beads into the nucleus and hung three yellow beads on the rings, because yellow was the colour he had the most of. Now that she said it, the whole thing looked flat, like a drawing with only one pencil.

"The label sheet says each particle gets its own colour," he said. He found the paper in his pocket. Protons, it read, were the ones in the nucleus with positive charge. Electrons were the ones on the rings with negative charge. The third kind, neutrons, sat in the nucleus too, and the line after that made him stop. "Neutrons have no charge at all."

Sara read over his shoulder. "No charge? Then how do you colour nothing?"

The whole model seemed to hinge on that one bead. Three protons, Brayden counted, and three electrons, and four neutrons. If he couldn't tell the neutrons apart from the protons, the judges would look at his nucleus and see seven identical beads and no thinking behind them. The差别 between the nucleus particles couldn't be seen directly, only implied by colour, and right now his colours implied nothing.

He tried an idea. "Positive could be red," he said slowly, pulling a red bead from his pouch. "Then electrons are blue on the rings. Opposite colours for opposite charges." He wired the red beads in and hung three blue ones. That left the neutrons.

"What colour is nothing?" Sara asked again.

Brayden looked around the gym. Then it landed on him. He took a black marker and painted four beads solid black. "Black," he said. "No charge, no colour."

Mr. Ba stopped at the table on his judge rounds and studied the model for a long moment. "Walk me through the nucleus," he said.

"Three red protons, positive," Brayden said, pointing. "Three blue electrons out here, negative. And four black neutrons."

"Which have no charge at all," Mr. Ba finished, and made a note on his clipboard. "Now that's a radical improvement from where you started, I'd guess."

He moved on to the volcano, and Sara whispered, "You're welcome." Brayden tilted the shoebox so the light caught the little black beads, then picked up the label sheet and wrote one word beside each colour.

activity: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
knowledge_domain: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
fact: Many stores stock shelves 'first in, first out', putting older products at the front, so the carton with the latest date is often at the back.
story:
Elijah held the envelope with exactly four dollars and fifty cents, one side of it rubbed soft from being folded and unfolded all morning. Mr. Virtanen had given the class a real-world assignment: walk to the corner store alone, buy one carton of milk, count the change, and bring back a receipt. "You'll modify your plan if something goes wrong," Mr. Virtanen said, "that's the whole point." Coraline, who had gone last week, winked at Elijah as they left. "Check the milk before you pay," she said, and nothing more, which was not helpful at all.

At the store, Elijah found the dairy case and reached for the front carton, then stopped. He had heard Coraline's warning in his head all afternoon, and now he noticed something. Every carton had a date stamped near the top, and the dates in the front row were different from the ones behind. He pulled one from the front and one from the back and compared them. The back one had the later date. He checked another pair. Later again. So that was what she meant: the store put older milk at the front, and the carton with the latest date was often at the back. Somebody had told Coraline that once, and now Elijah had seen it for himself. He slid his hand past the front row and took the freshest carton, feeling clever, like the store's system was a camouflage he had seen straight through.

At the register, the cashier said the milk was four dollars and nineteen cents. Elijah counted out the coins, then counted the change she handed back, coin by coin on the counter, the way he had practiced with Mr. Virtanen. Thirty-one cents. He said thank you, pocketed the receipt, and walked out with the milk hugged against his jacket.

Back at school, he showed the receipt to Mr. Virtanen, who nodded slowly. "And the milk?" Elijah turned the carton so the date faced him and pointed to it. "Got the newest one in the case." Coraline appeared beside them and smiled. "See? I told you to check." "You could have just said reach for the back," Elijah said, and she laughed. "You found it yourself. That's better." Mr. Virtanen gave an eloquent little wave of his hand toward the door. "Same assignment next month," he said. "Different aisle."

activity: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places
knowledge_domain: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places
fact: The most common kind of hydrogen atom has just one proton and one electron and no neutron at all.
story:
Gavin had claimed the corner of the garage his dad was still paying the mortgage on, and turned it into a lab. On Saturday morning he laid out his supplies with meticulous care: a foam ball for the proton, a tiny bead for the electron, and three pipe cleaners for the electron paths. Cadence sat cross-legged on an overturned bucket, reading the assignment aloud from Ms. Nielsen's handout.

"Build any atom," Cadence read. "Protons and neutrons in the nucleus, electrons outside it." Gavin had planned lithium, which meant hunting down six extra balls, but he'd lent his whole bag of foam to his cousin and the craft store's rules prohibited anyone under twelve from buying the glue he needed without a parent along. He slumped against the workbench. His whole project was stuck.

Then he remembered the chart in his science book. He flipped it open on the dusty floor and ran his finger down the first column. "Cadence, look," he said slowly. "Hydrogen. The most common kind has one proton and one electron. And no neutron at all. Nothing in the middle except the proton." He tested the idea out loud: if that was true, his single foam ball was already a complete nucleus. "I had it backwards. I thought every atom needed neutrons to hold it together. The chart says hydrogen just doesn't have any."

He pushed the bead onto a pipe-cleaner loop and hung it around the foam ball. Cadence held it up to the garage window, and the bead caught the light as it spun. That afternoon Gavin wrote a note to his cousin: "I need my foam balls back, but not for lithium anymore. I only ever needed one. Bring the bag Tuesday and I'll show you why the smallest atom in the universe is hiding in my garage." Cadence stuck the note in an envelope and drew an arrow on it, pointing at the little sun of pipe cleaner and foam. "Address it to the smartest kid on the block," she said, "because that's you now."

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Feeling anxious sometimes is normal, but when anxiety is intense, lasts a long time and gets in the way of daily life, a doctor may diagnose an anxiety disorder, which is treatable.
story:
Dominic sat on his bedroom floor with his back against the bed, holding his phone in both hands like it might bite him. On the screen, Jaycob's face filled the little square window, one eyebrow up. "So are you coming to Darius's thing on Saturday or not? I've asked three times. I'm doing a census of the whole grade and you're the only no."

Dominic looked at the poster of the eccentric old astronomer on his wall, the one with wild white hair and a telescope aimed at nothing. He liked the poster because the man looked like he did not care what anyone thought. That was the opposite of Dominic lately. "I don't know," he said. "My stomach hurts when I think about it. It's been hurting for like two weeks. Everything feels loud, even when it's quiet in here."

Jaycob leaned closer to the camera. "Two weeks? Dude. My cousin had that. She stopped sleeping, stopped eating basically, and it got in the way of school and everything. My mom said feeling anxious sometimes is normal, everybody gets that. But when it's really intense and it lasts a long time and it stops you doing normal stuff, a doctor can diagnose an anxiety disorder." He shrugged. "That's the actual word, anxiety disorder. And it's treatable. My cousin told a doctor, and she's way better now. She still has stress, but she has ways of coping with it."

Dominic turned the phone over in his hands. He had been telling himself the stomach aches were from the cafeteria pizza, or from staying up too late. But the pizza theory did not fit the pattern: the ache showed up on school nights and on Saturday mornings before parties, and never during the horror movie marathon last weekend. Maybe he had been looking for the wrong hidden cause. He thought about the last party, in this same room, where he had spent an hour deciding what to say to Darius and then said nothing. He could not change that night, but he was still holding it, letting it consume whole evenings.

"Can you even do anything about it, though?" he asked. "I can't just tell my brain to stop."

"You tell the doctor, not your brain," Jaycob said. "That's the whole move. And you set boundaries, like, you don't have to go Saturday. A no is allowed. My cousin says that all the time."

Dominic stood up, walked to his window, and pushed it open. Cold air smelling of cut grass rushed in. Down the street a leaf blower growled and somewhere a dog barked twice. He could hear his mom in the kitchen below, stacking dishes.

"Okay," he said into the phone. "I'll ask my mom to make a doctor thing. And put me down as maybe for Saturday." He paused at the door. "Hey Mom? Can we talk about something?"

activity: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
knowledge_domain: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
fact: When two identical bulbs are wired in series to one battery, each glows more dimly than a single bulb would on the same battery.
story:
Bennett had chosen the lighthouse on purpose. His social studies class had read about refugee families crossing dark seas, and he wanted his model to show how a lighthouse says "land is here" to someone who has nowhere safe to go. He'd spent two evenings wiring it: a battery, a switch, a bulb in the tower. On Friday he pressed the switch, and the little light glowed steady and bright. Perfect.

Then Kaylin walked past his table at the science fair and stopped. "It's good," she said, "but one bulb? A contemporary lighthouse has a big lamp, not a tiny one. Add a second bulb. Two has to be brighter than one." Bennett looked at his tower. Two lights, one above the other, would look stronger. He had a spare identical bulb in his parts box, so he unscrewed the lamp cover and wired the second bulb into the same path, one after the other.

He flipped the switch. Both bulbs lit, but each one glowed more dimly than his single bulb had glowed on the same battery. Bennett stared. He checked the wires, wiggled the connections, even swapped in a fresh battery from his pocket. Still dim, both of them, together. He whispered, "That's backwards."

Kael leaned over from the next table. "What's backwards?" Bennett explained: one bulb on this battery, bright; two identical bulbs wired in a row, dimmer, each of them. Kael suggested they eliminate the switch in case it was the problem, so they took it out and joined the wires directly. Nothing changed. Both bulbs still glowed with less light than either one alone would have shown. "Then it's not the switch," Kael said slowly. "It's the two bulbs themselves."

In his lunch bag Bennett found the note his grandfather had tucked there that morning, because Grandpa couldn't come to the fair. "Dear Bennett," it read, "your grandmother says to tell you: the lamp does not have to be big to be brave. It only has to stay lit. Love, Grandpa." Bennett read it twice, then went back to his table.

He unscrewed the second bulb, reconnected the first one straight to the battery, and replaced the switch. When the judge, Mr. Rahman, stopped at his table, Bennett pressed it. The single bulb glowed bright and steady inside the tower. "One bulb, one battery, one switch," Bennett said. "The electricity goes around in one loop, and when I open the switch, the loop is broken and the light goes out." Mr. Rahman nodded and wrote something on his clipboard. Behind the bright little window, Bennett taped his grandfather's note where only he could see it.

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: Knowing a word's language of origin can help with spelling: the 'k' sound in 'chorus' is spelled 'ch' because it comes from Greek, while the 'sh' in 'chef' comes from French.
story:
The regional spelling bee had gone online this year, so Alexia sat at her kitchen table with the laptop propped on a stack of cookbooks while her dad hovered behind her with the vacuum switched off. Down in the corner of the screen, in a grid of tiny faces, Yousuf gave her a thumbs up. He had made it to the finals too, and all week they had drilled each other over video calls after homework. His one wish was to beat his older sister's record from three years ago, when she had placed fourth, and he reminded Alexia of it at least twice a day.

Round four began, and the announcer called her name. "Alexia, your word is chef." She asked for the definition, then for the language of origin. "French," the announcer said. Alexia spelled it c-h-e-f, and it was correct, but her stomach still felt tight, because the next word could be anything.

Between rounds, waiting was anything but leisure for her; she kept her hands busy straightening the pencils on the table. Then she noticed something. When the announcer had said French for chef, the sh sound at the start had been spelled with the letters c and h. She remembered Yousuf's practice list, and the word chorus, where the same letters c and h made a k sound. She had missed chorus in a practice round on Tuesday, spelling it with a plain k. Maybe the difference wasn't luck. Maybe the language of origin was the hidden key, and she could test it if the chance came.

"Alexia, your word is chimera." She asked for the definition first, buying a second to think. Then she asked, "Language of origin?" "Greek," the announcer said. Greek, like chorus. If the pattern held, that k sound at the start would be spelled with c and h. She imagined Yousuf on the other side of the screen, mouthing breathe, which is what he always mouthed at her. She started the word slowly, letter by letter, c-h-i-m-e-r-a, and held her breath until the bell that meant wrong stayed silent.

"Correct," the announcer said, and the moderator's voice added that the next round was imminent. In the corner of the grid, Yousuf's face lit up; he had advanced too, which meant his sister's record was still within reach for him. The pronouncer turned to his list. "Yousuf, your word is charisma." Yousuf leaned toward his camera, and Alexia heard him ask, calm and steady, "Language of origin, please?"

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: A canoe is most stable when paddlers keep their weight low and centered, which is why people step into the middle of a canoe rather than onto its side.
story:
Theo stood at the end of the lakeside dock with his duffel bag at his feet, because in exactly one hour the camp van would carry him away for a whole month. Before he left, he wanted one thing: to paddle a canoe, just once, so he wouldn't be the only beginner at camp.

Zaid held the canoe steady against the dock while Luciana sat in the middle seat, paddle across her knees. Theo grabbed the gunwale and swung his leg over the side. The instant his sneaker touched the canoe's edge, the whole boat tipped like a seesaw, and cold lake water slopped over the rim. He jerked back onto the dock, heart hammering.

"That wasn't random," Theo said slowly, watching the canoe rock. "It tipped exactly where I stepped." He thought about Luciana, sitting low and centered, who had barely wobbled at all. Was there a rule hiding in that? He tested it, putting his foot not on the edge but into the middle of the hull, right where Luciana's pack lay flat. The canoe swayed a little, then settled, steady as a table.

"So that's why people step into the middle of a canoe and not onto its side," he said. "The weight has to be low and centered. That's what keeps it stable."

"Your intuition is better than mine was," Zaid admitted. "I fell in last summer. Twice."

Mr. Bondarenko, whose dock it was, ambled down and helped Theo acquire a paddle from the boathouse rack, checking the life jacket straps himself before letting them push off. For twenty minutes the three of them glided past the reeds, Theo crouched low in the center, learning to steer.

When the van finally honked from the road, Theo ran up the hill, waving. "First thing I'm telling everyone at camp," he called back over his shoulder, "is I already know where to step!"

activity: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
knowledge_domain: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
fact: Lines of longitude meet at the poles, so a degree of longitude spans about 111 kilometers at the equator but shrinks to zero at the poles.
story:
Elizabeth had exactly forty minutes before her flight to Denver, and one enormous problem: she had promised her grandmother she would send the location of every city she visited, written in latitude and longitude, because Grandma wanted to pin them all on a wall map. The only trouble was that Elizabeth had never read latitude and longitude in her life.

She spread the atlas she'd bought at the airport bookstore across two plastic chairs near gate B12, and her friend Desiree leaned over it, cracking gum. "Numbers everywhere," Desiree said. "Which ones are the city?"

"That's what we're finding out." Elizabeth traced her finger across the curved lines. The ones running sideways, wrapping around the world like belts, had to be latitude, because she remembered Ms. Sokolov saying the equator was latitude zero. So the lines stretching from top to bottom, like segments of an orange, were longitude. Denver sat near the number 105 on one of those tall lines. "Thirty-nine north, one hundred five west," she read aloud. "That's Denver."

Then Ayah arrived with a paper cup of hot chocolate and a globe from the gift shop, a frail little thing she was afraid to fracture if she dropped it, which was why she carried it like a baby bird. "Look at the top," Ayah said, spinning it slowly. Elizabeth bent close. Near the equator, the longitude lines stood far apart, but near the top of the globe they squeezed together, crowding in like roads merging until they all touched at a single point.

"They meet," Elizabeth whispered. "At the pole, they actually touch." She grabbed the ruler from her backpack and measured on the map's scale bar. "At the equator, one degree of longitude is about a hundred eleven kilometers. But up at the pole it has to shrink to zero, because the lines have run out of room. Zero!" She checked the atlas key, and there it was in print, exactly what she'd worked out. She felt like a detective who had solved the case before the police.

Desiree wrote the Denver coordinates on a napkin and then, since they had twenty minutes left, they hunted down Tokyo, Nairobi, and Reykjavik, whose longitude lines were packed so tightly toward the top that Elizabeth had to squint. "Grandma's going to need a bigger map," she said, copying the last one down.

The speaker crackled with her boarding call. Elizabeth snapped the atlas shut, hugged both friends, and jogged toward the gate, napkin held high like a flag.

"Send us Reykjavik!" Ayah called after her.

"Already on it!" Elizabeth shouted over her shoulder.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: In a fair test, everything except the variable being tested is kept the same, such as the amount, the temperature and the timing.
story:
Brielle taped her last poster word, "HYPOTHESIS," just as Ms. Mendoza opened the gym doors and the science fair began. Her project claimed that a paper airplane with wide wings would glide farther than one with narrow wings. "That's my testable guess," she told Heather, who was guarding the two planes at the table. "If the wide one wins, my guess holds up. If not, it's overturned."

But when Brielle demonstrated, the wide-winged plane nosedived and the narrow one sailed. Heather laughed so hard she knocked over the cup of pennies they were using as table currency for counting trial runs. Something felt wrong to Brielle, and she thought back to last Saturday, when she had folded the wide plane at her kitchen table and thrown it in the still hallway. It had glided beautifully then, past the laundry basket and onto the couch. So what had changed? She looked around the gym and noticed the propped-open door, and the draft of wind rattling the endangered spider plant on the windowsill, one gust away from losing its last three leaves.

"You can't compare them like this," she said. "In a fair test, everything except the thing you're testing has to be kept the same. Same amount of paper, same throws, and same wind, which means none. The wide one just flew into a breeze." Emy-Jade wandered over from the moldy-bread exhibit and offered to stand guard by the door until Ms. Mendoza could authorize closing it, since only adults were allowed to touch the doors during the fair.

Brielle re-threw both planes in the still air, ten careful trials each. The wide wings won eight times out of ten. Her hypothesis had survived after all, once the sneaky wind was taken out of the picture. She crossed out the word "overturned" on her poster and wrote "supported," then held up the wide plane like a tiny silver trophy.

"Ladies and gentlemen," she announced to Heather and Emy-Jade, "never trust a gym with a draft."

activity: to hurdle a row of low hurdles with a three-step rhythm between them
knowledge_domain: to hurdle a row of low hurdles with a three-step rhythm between them
fact: Hurdlers take off farther from a hurdle than they land after it; taking off too close forces the lead knee up steeply and slows them down.
story:
Benjamin stood at the start of the row of low hurdles, and his heart was doing the three-step rhythm before his feet were. "Film it again," he begged Shaan, who was crouched by lane four with his phone. Shaan wanted to make the practice highlight reel for the class channel, and he had already built a whole database of clips, tagging each one with Benjamin's times, so nothing about this could stay a secret for long.

"Go on then," Shaan said. Benjamin ran. One, two, three, hurdle. One, two, three, hurdle. His lead knee cracked the third barrier, and the fifth, and he crossed the finish in a tangle of white plastic. Ms. Chatterjee blew her whistle and jogged over, but she only said, "Watch your own video, not my mouth," because that was the rule she had made mandatory for learning new events: figure it out before being told.

They crowded around the phone behind the equipment shed. Brynlee, who had come to time him because she wanted the official numbers for her stopwatch notebook, leaned in too. Benjamin scrubbed the clip backwards and forwards, watching his own legs. There it was. He took off close to each hurdle, and his lead knee shot straight up like a drawbridge, stiff and slow, and that was exactly when he clipped the bar. But on the one hurdle he cleared cleanly, he had pushed off farther back and landed just past it, close on the far side. "Look," he said, jabbing the screen. "I take off way farther away than I land after. When I crowd it, my knee has to go up all steep and it slows me down." Brynlee read out the splits to prove it: the clean hurdle was his fastest split of all.

He walked back to the line, counted his steps out loud, and planted a cone in the grass where the good takeoff had been. "Brynlee, accompany me to lane four," he said grandly, holding out his hand like an announcer. "Somebody has to catch the record."

Shaan hit record. "Three, two, one," he called, and Benjamin flew.

activity: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places
knowledge_domain: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places
fact: In the gold foil experiment, run by Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden under Ernest Rutherford, most alpha particles passed straight through, showing an atom is mostly empty space.
story:
Elena pressed one more gold bead onto her foam sphere and stepped back to look at it. Her model of a gold atom was completely covered, every centimeter packed with beads for protons and neutrons, with electrons glued around the outside like sprinkles. It had taken three evenings, and tomorrow was the science fair, where the winning project would go on to a prestigious regional contest.

"You did the whole thing already?" Prisha set her own half-built skeleton of pipe cleaners on the table beside Elena's. "Mine still looks like a collapsed tent."

"It was supposed to be a collaboration," Darcy said, arriving with the glue gun and a wounded expression. "You said Saturday."

"I know. I got carried away." Elena turned the sphere so Darcy could see the gap where one bead had popped off. "You can do the electron rings. I saved them."

Mr. Johansson paused at their table on his rounds of the gym, coffee cup in hand. He tilted his head at the solid ball of beads. "Interesting. Have you read about the gold foil experiment?"

Elena shook her head, and he moved on to the next table without another word, which felt like a challenge.

At the library after school, she found it. Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden, working under Ernest Rutherford, had fired tiny particles at gold foil, and most of the alpha particles passed straight through. Elena read the page twice. Passed through gold. Atoms were mostly empty space. She stared at her packed, crowded sphere, heavy as a bowling ball in her lap, and felt like the whole thing was a small rebellion against how the universe actually worked.

The next morning she pried off the beads with a butter knife, and Prisha knelt on the other side and caught them in a cup. Darcy threaded the three of them that remained onto clear fishing line, so the nucleus hung in the middle of a wire frame with nothing but air around it. The electrons went on the outer rings, small and alone in all that space.

At the fair, a judge leaned close to the frame. "So where's the rest of it?"

"That is the rest of it," Elena said. "In the gold foil experiment, most alpha particles passed straight through the foil, because an atom is mostly empty space."

The judge smiled and moved on, and Prisha squeezed Elena's elbow. Down the row, Mr. Johansson gave them a small nod from behind his coffee cup.

activity: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
knowledge_domain: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
fact: The equilibrium price is the price at which the amount buyers want to buy equals the amount sellers want to sell.
story:
Alicia had one job at the mall's spring market: help Agnes and Liliana sell strawberries at their little table by the fountain, and figure out one thing for her social studies sheet. The question was why strawberries cost less in summer than in winter. She had a hunch it had something to do with how many boxes people would buy, but a hunch wasn't an answer, and the sheet was due Monday.

The morning was slow and tedious, mostly straightening boxes and watching shoppers revolve past on the escalator without stopping. The sign said two dollars a box, and by lunch they had sold only six of forty. Agnes slumped onto the stool. "We're going to carry all these home."

"Then the price is wrong," Alicia said. She was guessing, but it was a guess she could test. "Summer strawberries are cheap, so cheap that people buy tons of them. Let's try one dollar." Liliana found the marker in the craft bag, crossed out the two, and they waited.

It worked almost too well. By two o'clock half the boxes were gone, and by four there were only eight left with an hour of market time to go. Alicia counted the boxes, then the customers drifting by, then the clock above the jewelry store. Some shoppers picked up a box, saw the price, and put it back. Others carried off two at a time. Buyers wanting to buy and sellers wanting to sell, she thought, were like two sides of a seesaw. When the two sides matched, everything balanced.

"Raise it to one fifty," she said. At one fifty, the last eight boxes went slowly, one at a time, to a woman with a stroller, to Ms. Hoang from the music store downstairs, who bought two and said the girl at the next table should save the last box for her. Agnes held it behind the register, and at exactly five o'clock, closing time, the woman came back, and the table was empty. Nothing left over, nothing carried home.

Liliana wrote on the sheet: the price where the amount buyers want to buy equals the amount sellers want to sell. "There's a name for it," Agnes said, flipping through the handout. "Equilibrium price."

"So winter strawberries are expensive because at a high price, the small number of boxes matches the smaller number of buyers," Alicia said, stacking the empty crates. "And summer strawberries are cheap because there are so many of both." Ms. Hoang tucked her box into her tote and smiled at the three of them.

"Now we just need something to sell next month," Liliana said. "Something that runs out exactly at closing time."

activity: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
knowledge_domain: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
fact: To subtract fractions with unlike denominators, rewrite both with a common denominator first: three quarters minus one third becomes nine twelfths minus four twelfths, which is five twelfths.
story:
Hunter dragged the chair across the kitchen and climbed up to the top shelf, where his mom kept the craft box. Moving the old calendars exposed a spool of red ribbon, exactly what he needed for the model bridge due tomorrow. He measured off three quarters of a metre and cut it, then held the roll up to the window. Not much left. He set the piece on the table beside his sketch.

The problem was the sketch itself. It showed a span, two towers, and a strip of ribbon running along the top, but Eliot had called ten minutes ago with news that had made Hunter's stomach drop. "The suspension cable has to be a third of a metre," Eliot had said, "and the anchor cables come off the same piece. Mr. Nair measured them in class today with the metre stick." Their piece was three quarters of a metre. A third went to the span. Would the rest cover the anchors, or was the whole project sunk?

Hunter did not want to cut anything until he knew. He pulled his math notebook toward him and wrote 3/4 minus 1/3. The numbers just sat there, refusing to line up. Fourths were not thirds; he could picture the cut marks on the ribbon, and they did not match up anywhere. He tried counting on his fingers and got nowhere. Outside, a storm was rolling in, and the kitchen light flickered once, which made him feel like the clock was against him too.

Then he thought of the measuring cup. His mom used it for rice, and it had marks all around the inside: halves, thirds, fourths, and a fine set of little lines between them. He found it in the drawer and turned it slowly under the tap light. If he poured to a fourth, the water touched one of the small lines. If he poured to a third, it touched another. He counted the small lines carefully, twice. Twelfths. Every mark on the cup was a twelfth, and both of his fractions landed on them.

Back at the table, he wrote it out. Three quarters was equivalent to nine twelfths. One third was equivalent to four twelfths. Nine twelfths minus four twelfths came to five twelfths of a metre left over after the span. Five twelfths was almost half a metre, and his sketch needed only about a quarter metre of anchor cables. His pencil hovered over the paper while he checked the counting one last time, because if he was wrong, there was no second piece of ribbon in the house.

He cut a third of a metre for the span, then laid the leftover along the ruler. Five twelfths. He measured out the anchor cables, and there was still ribbon to spare. His phone buzzed. "Did you figure it out, or are we building a plank bridge?" Eliot asked. Hunter wrapped the extra ribbon around his finger and grinned at the window, where the first fat raindrops were hitting the glass. "Suspension bridge," he said. "Come over and bring the popsicle sticks."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Acrylic paint is thinned with water while wet, but once it dries it becomes water-resistant, so brushes must be washed before the paint dries on them.
story:
Stella spread the canvas boards across the picnic table in Gunnar's backyard and counted the brushes in the jar. Three of them stood stiff as sticks, their bristles frozen into sharp little points. She had left them in the studio overnight, and now the mural for Ms. Wiśniewski's community garden sign was due at five o'clock, and it was already noon.

"Soak them in hot water," Gunnar said, filling a bucket from the garden hose. "That always works."

Stella dipped one brush in and swirled it. Nothing happened. The bristles stayed frozen, and when she pressed them against her palm they left a hard line, like a stick of chalk. She thought about what she'd noticed while painting yesterday: the paint had rinsed off her hands easily while it was wet, but the smudge she'd missed on her sleeve had hardened and survived the washing machine. She turned that over in her head. If the paint thinned with water only while it was wet, then once it dried it must resist water completely. That would explain why soaking was doing nothing at all.

"Hot water isn't going to fix these," she said. "The paint already dried on them. Water can't get it off once it's dry."

"That's not a credible plan," Gunnar said. "We need three working brushes for the lettering."

"Then we test it my way first." Stella held a stiff brush under the tap and squeezed dish soap into the bristles, working it in with her fingers, then rinsed. A thin ribbon of softened paint came out, but the core stayed hard. She tried a second time, scrubbing harder, and more came free, but the bristles splayed crooked.

"Two minutes," Reese called from the porch, where she'd been waiting to help with the vines. "My mom said she can drive the sign over to the garden at five, but she has to commute to her evening shift right after, so there's no second trip."

Stella looked at the two clean brushes left in the jar, then at the painted letters already finished, then at the long border of leaves still undone. The landlord who owned the garden plot had promised the sign would hang by the gate this weekend, and half the neighborhood would see it.

"Gunnar, I changed my mind," she said. "Forget the stiff ones. We each take a clean brush and do the leaves together. And after this, we wash the brushes right away, before anything dries. Every time."

They painted fast, trading the water cup between them, dipping and rinsing and rinsing again. By four thirty the border was done, green leaves curling around the letters. Stella carried the brushes straight to the hose and washed them under the cold stream until the water ran clear, then laid them flat on the table to dry in the sun.

Reese held up the finished sign. "Ms. Wiśniewski is going to hang this by the gate tonight."

"Then let's get it in the car before anything else dries on us," Stella said, and she picked up the brushes to keep.

activity: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing
knowledge_domain: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing
fact: In front crawl, swimmers breathe out underwater through the mouth and nose, so they only need a quick breath in when the face turns to the side.
story:
Blake stood at the shallow end of the community pool that shared a building with the hockey rink, listening to the thud of pucks hitting the boards through the wall. Twenty-five metres. That was the whole test, and he had failed it twice, always in the same way.

"Same spot every time," said Mathieu, hanging on the lane rope. "Between the flags and the wall. You turn your head, cough like a seal, and stand up."

"I'm trying to get a big enough breath," Blake said. He wasn't lying. He turned his face to the side, tried to let the old air out and pull new air in during that one quick moment, and every time the water won. It poured into his mouth, and that was that.

Calla swam past them, slow and easy, her face rolling to the side like it was nothing. Blake watched her go. She wasn't taking a huge breath. He could see that much. Her mouth barely opened at all. So why did she have air to spare?

Mr. Dlamini, the lifeguard on duty, blew his whistle at two kids trying to obstruct the lap lane with a pool noodle, and Blake kept watching Calla's face underwater. A stream of bubbles came out of her nose and mouth the whole time her face was down. Then when she turned, she only had to breathe in. One thing, not two things.

"That's it," Blake said. He pushed off before he could talk himself out of it. Face in, he pushed the air out through his mouth and nose, a steady fizz of bubbles, and when his arm pulled back he rolled his head, took one quick sip of air, and put his face down again. Bubbles out. Sip in. The flags went by overhead. Then the wall was under his hand.

He stood up, breathing hard but not coughing.

"You got the tutor after all," Mathieu said, grinning. "Calla's been showing you stuff all week."

"I figured it out myself," Blake said, but not in a defiant way. He looked down the lane. "Mostly."

Calla laughed and pushed off toward the deep end. "Race you to twenty-five," she called over her shoulder.

Blake shoved off the wall after her.

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: In Mexican tradition, a quinceañera, the celebration of a girl's fifteenth birthday, usually begins with a Mass of thanksgiving.
story:
Maeva stood in her grandmother's kitchen with the folded paper in her hand, reading the same line for the tenth time. In two days she would stand in front of everyone at her cousin's quinceañera and deliver the reading at the Mass, and so far she could only get through three sentences without stumbling.

"Taha says he memorized a whole speech once by recording it and playing it while he slept," said Olivia, who was sitting on the counter eating an orange. "You could try that tonight."

"Two nights," Maeva said. "That's not enough sleep to learn two paragraphs." She stared at the paper. Something was wrong with her method, and she tried to figure out what. She had been rereading the words from the top every time, so the beginning was smooth and the ending was shaky. The problem, she realized, wasn't the words themselves. It was that she only ever practiced the easy part first. When she stood up in church, she would have to start at the beginning with no warm-up, so she needed a way to practice starting cold.

"It would be logical to begin in a different place every time," she said slowly. "Random spots. Middle of paragraph two. Last line. Then the beginning would just be one more starting point, not the only one."

"Or," said Olivia, "you could panic, which is what I would do."

Grandma shuffled in with the mop and told them to lift their feet. "Two more days until the big one," she said. "Your mother made a whole controversy out of the cake flavors, can you believe it. Vanilla or tres leches, and now half the family isn't speaking to the other half."

Maeva closed her eyes and recited from the middle of the second paragraph, the part she always fumbled. The words came out clean. She opened her eyes and grinned. "It's working."

They spent the next hour testing each other. Olivia would call out a line, and Maeva would take off from there, sometimes fast, sometimes slow, once while hopping on one foot because Olivia claimed distraction training would accelerate her progress. Grandma declared it the strangest rehearsal she had ever mopped around.

On Saturday morning, in her grandmother's front room, Maeva smoothed her dress one last time. The church organ started. She took a breath and began, and the first sentence came out steady and sure, right on cue, as if she had started there a hundred times before. Somewhere in the third pew, Olivia gave her a thumbs up.

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: Judgment words such as best, worst, beautiful, boring and should are often signs that a sentence expresses an opinion.
story:
Camille slouched at the lunch table, poking at her noodles while Hayden flipped through a stack of crumpled papers. "Ms. Pham wants us to find five checkable facts in these product reviews by tomorrow," Hayden groaned. "But every sentence says stuff like best or boring, and I can't tell what counts."

Camille pulled one review toward her. It was for a metal water bottle, and the reviewer had written in fat, cheerful handwriting. She read it aloud under her breath. "This is the best bottle I've ever owned. It holds twenty-four ounces. The lid leaks. You should buy the purple one. The design is beautiful." Something about the words snagged in her mind, the way a thread catches on a splinter. She grabbed Hayden's green highlighter and dragged it across "best," then "boring" in the next review, then "should," then "beautiful," then "worst." When she circled what was left, only a few thin sentences remained, holding an amount of liquid, a leaking lid, a color. She looked up slowly. "Judgment words like best, worst, beautiful, boring and should are often signals that a sentence is an opinion, not a fact."

Hayden leaned over, chewing the cap of a pen. "So the leak we could test? Actually test?" That was the idea that had lain dormant in Camille's head since morning, and now it woke up. She reached into her backpack and pulled out her own purple water bottle, the same brand as the review. She filled it at the water fountain in the hallway, listening to the cold stream plink against the metal, then screwed the lid on tight, flipped it upside down over a paper towel, and counted. At ten seconds the towel stayed dry. At thirty, one dark dot bloomed near the rim.

"That's our checkable claim," Camille said, her stomach doing a small flip of excitement. "The review said it leaks. It does. That's not opinion, that's something anybody could test." Kash wandered over from the vending machines with a bag of pretzels and read the highlighted pages upside down. "You turned opinions into a treasure map," he said. "The judgments govern nothing. The leftover sentences are where the facts hide."

That evening Camille wrote a note and slipped it into Hayden's locker before the buses were called.

Hayden, I checked. Best, worst, boring, beautiful, should, all highlighted, all signals of opinion. Everything left over in all three reviews was testable: twenty-four ounces (I measured mine with the kitchen measuring cup), leaky lid (confirmed, upside-down test, thirty seconds), purple color (confirmed, looked at it). Five facts found, no guessing. Bring your highlighter tomorrow. Camille.

In class the next morning, Ms. Pham walked between the desks, tapping the pages. When she reached Camille and Hayden, she picked up their sheet, studied the green stripes and the neat circles, and raised her eyebrows. "You found the pattern yourself?" Camille nodded, and Hayden pointed at the highlighted "best" in the first line. "That word tried to trick us," Hayden said. Ms. Pham smiled and set the page back down. "Then read us your favorite checkable claim," she said. Camille took a breath and stood up.

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: In a healthy onion cell, the cell membrane is pressed tightly against the inside of the cell wall, which makes the membrane very hard to see as a separate line.
story:
Eva set the microscope on the picnic table and weighted the instructions with a pinecone so the wind couldn't take them. Mr. Asante had lent her the scope for the weekend along with three slides, a razor blade in a folded paper sleeve, and a single demand: draw one onion cell and label the cell wall, the cell membrane, and the nucleus. "Extra credit," he had said, "but only if all three labels are there."

Violet arrived on her bike with an onion from her mother's kitchen, and Cade came over the fence the way he always did, dropping into the grass without using the gate. Eva peeled a thin layer from the inner curve of the onion, the layer so fine it looked like fog, and laid it on the slide. Under the lowest lens the cells appeared like a brick wall, each one a neat rectangle with a darker dot near the middle. "Nucleus," she said, and wrote it. The outer edge of each brick was plain too, a firm line all the way around. She wrote "cell wall."

Then she sat back and frowned. The assignment called for three labels, and she had two. There was no second line anywhere inside the rectangles, nothing between the wall and the inside of the cell. "Maybe onions just don't have one," Cade said, chewing a blade of grass. "Mr. Asante wouldn't ask for it if it didn't exist," Violet said. "He's not like that."

Eva turned the fine focus very slowly, watching the edge of one cell. She remembered how the squash had looked when she'd forgotten to water it, how its skin had pulled away from the flesh in a loose ridge. What if the membrane was there but hidden, pressed flat against the inside of the cell wall so tightly that it couldn't show as a separate line? She couldn't see that directly. But she could test it. If something made the cell lose water, would the membrane pull away from the wall and become visible?

"What could make it shrink?" she asked. Violet suggested salt, and Cade told an anecdote about his grandmother sprinkling salt on cucumber slices and watching puddles form within minutes, which made his point better than any argument. Eva fetched a glass of water from the kitchen, stirred in a spoonful of salt, and let the slide sit in a shallow dish of it. They waited, swatting mosquitoes, while the sprinkler next door made its vigorous sweep across the neighbor's lawn.

When she looked again, she leaned so close her braid fell against the stage. Inside several cells the membrane had drawn back from the wall, curling inward like a deflating balloon, and now it stood out as its own clear line. She drew one cell twice, before and after, and labeled the membrane on the second drawing with an arrow and a note: pressed tight against the wall normally, you only see it when the cell shrinks. "So it was there the whole time," Cade said, peering into the eyepiece. Eva took the slide off the stage and held it up to the light, looking at the thin wet sheet that had kept its secret until the salt asked the question.

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A claim can be checkable even if nobody has checked it yet; 'most students at our school walk to school' could be tested with a survey.
story:
At dinner Leah pushed her noodles around her plate and said, "Deklan told everyone today that most students at our school walk to school. Ms. Krause asked him how he knew, and he just said everybody does, obviously. But does everybody? I see bikes jammed into the rack every morning."

Her dad set down his fork. "So is he wrong?"

"That's the thing. I don't know if he's wrong. That's what's bugging me." She pulled the folded paper out of her pocket and smoothed it beside her glass. "Ellia said it's just his opinion and opinions can't be wrong. But it doesn't feel like an opinion. An opinion is like when I say the cafeteria pizza is better than the pasta. Nobody can check that. Deklan said a fact about how many kids walk, and that seems like something you could actually count."

"So count it," her dad said, spooning more sauce onto her noodles whether she wanted it or not.

Leah looked at the paper, where she had scrawled a tally grid on the bus ride home. Rows for walk, bike, car, bus. Empty columns. "That's what I was thinking. Ms. Krause postponed our quiz until Friday so we'd have time, actually. She said if we're going to argue about it, we should find out. I asked her how, and she said a survey would work, and that was all she'd tell us. Ellia and I figured out the rest after class." She tapped the grid. "We stand at the front doors tomorrow morning and mark one line per kid. Ellia takes the eighth graders, I take everyone else. Deklan, if he shows up, can count bikes, since he was so sure of himself."

"Seems fair," her dad said. "You know nobody's ever counted this before, right? You three could be the first."

Leah stopped, fork halfway to her mouth. She hadn't thought of that. "Huh. So right now, this minute, nobody in the world knows if Deklan's right?" The idea gave her a strange, fizzy feeling, like discovering an unopened room in a house she thought she knew. "I kept thinking a fact had to already be written down somewhere, in a book or on a website. But a thing can be checkable even if nobody has checked it yet." She said it slowly, testing it. "It's just sitting there waiting."

"It's like the dinosaurs," her dad said. "Their extinction wasn't a mystery forever. Somebody found the bones and checked."

"I guess." She was already folding the paper into quarters, then into eighths, so it would fit in her jacket pocket without ripping. At lunch she would get Ellia's answer about Deklan, and if he was in, all three of them would have to agree on the plan. She hoped it would be unanimous, because arguing took longer than counting, and she wanted to be at the doors by seven forty.

She ate a real bite of noodles at last. Tomorrow morning, one tally mark at a time, she was going to find out what was true.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: Naive realism is the belief that we see the world as it really is, so people who disagree with us must be uninformed or biased.
story:
Audrey set down the platter of noodles and listened to her grandfather start the lake story for what had to be the hundredth time. He claimed Aunt Rosa had shown up two hours late to the family reunion picnic and ruined the group photo. Her mother, ladling sauce, said no, Rosa had been exactly on time, and it was Grandpa who had wandered off to the dock and made everyone wait. They argued the way they always did, with the fond stubbornness of people who had been disagreeing for decades. Nicole, sitting beside Audrey with her napkin folded in her lap, raised her eyebrows.

"That's not even possible," Nicole whispered. "Someone has to be wrong."

Audrey had invited Nicole and Kyson over for dinner partly to escape homework and partly because her mother made better noodles than anyone, but now she had a new reason to be glad they'd come. For months she had been chewing on a question she couldn't digest: how could two people remember the same afternoon so differently and both be certain? Grandpa said Rosa ruined the photo. Mom said Grandpa did. Each of them thought the other was being unreasonable, and neither would budge.

She remembered a day in October when she had done the same thing. Nicole had borrowed her calculator and returned it with a cracked screen, and Audrey had spent a whole weekend certain that Nicole was careless and didn't care. Then Nicole showed her the dent in her backpack where a locker door had slammed shut on it. Audrey had felt her certainty tilt sideways, and the feeling had never fully settled back into place. Maybe everybody walked around like that, she thought, believing they saw things exactly as they were and assuming anyone who disagreed was just misinformed. She wanted to test it while everyone was still at the table.

"Grandpa," she said, "tell the story again, but pretend you're Aunt Rosa." He grumbled, but he tried it, describing himself waiting at the picnic tables while a man strolled off toward the water. Then Mom told it as Grandpa, watching the clock while Rosa's car finally pulled in. By the time the noodles were cold, each of them had paused at least once, and Mom laughed at her own version, which she had never done before.

"Mr. Foster calls that naive realism," Kyson said, reaching for the bread. "Thinking you see things as they really are, so anyone who disagrees must be uniformed or biased." He shrugged. "He says everybody does it."

Nicole turned her fork over. "So who's right about the lake?"

Nobody answered. Grandpa spooned more sauce onto his plate, and Mom went to the drawer for the old photo album, the one with the durable cracked spine, and set it down in the middle of the table.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Lunar New Year, celebrated in China, Korea, Vietnam and elsewhere, falls on a new moon between January 21 and February 20.
story:
Muhammad raced across the frosty park with a paper flyer flapping in his hand, weaving between the lanterns already being strung between the oak trees. The Lunar New Year festival started in two weeks, and his class project on family celebrations was due the day after the big dinner. There was just one problem: he had told Mr. Dlamini the project would be presented on February second, and now the flyer said the festival was January twenty-ninth.

"Corbin! Kingston!" he shouted, skidding to a stop at the picnic table where his friends were stacking paper lanterns for the volunteer booth. "The dinner is on the twenty-ninth. My whole project plan is wrong."

Corbin shrugged. "So move your plan. Big deal."

"You don't get it. Last year the dinner was in February. I remember because it was after my cousin's birthday." Muhammad flipped the flyer over, then pulled out his phone and opened the calendar app, thumbing back through months. January. He tapped the moon symbol again and again. "Every year it's different. It jumps around."

Kingston leaned over his shoulder. "My mom says it's the moon calendar. She's Korean, and her friends from Vietnam and China all celebrate the same day."

"Then it's a new moon thing," Muhammad said slowly. He scrolled back to last January and found it: a new moon, and the festival right on it. He scrolled to this January. Another new moon, late in the month. "It lands on a new moon between January twenty-one and February twenty. That's the rule. That's why it moves."

"Diagnosis: you planned your project around the wrong date," Kingston said, grinning. "Prescription: ask Mr. Dlamini to move it."

Muhammad had tried that already, sort of. On Monday he had stammered out a request and Mr. Dlamini had waved him off, saying the schedule was the schedule, notorious for never changing. This time Muhammad would bring proof. He spent the rest of the afternoon photographing the flyer, the calendar app, and the huge banner the volunteers had just finished hanging over the park gates, red and gold letters announcing the festival date.

On Monday he laid the pictures on Mr. Dlamini's desk before the teacher could dismiss him. "My family's dinner is on the twenty-ninth. New moon between January twenty-one and February twenty. I can't present after it happens, it won't make sense."

Mr. Dlamini studied the photos for a long moment, then looked up. "Move it up a week, then. And Muhammad?"

"Yes?"

"Bring mooncakes to the presentation."

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: 1 is not a prime number; mathematicians exclude it so that every whole number has only one way to be written as a product of primes.
story:
Charles had exactly forty minutes of coding club left, and his program still thought that 1 was prime. He had typed it himself: ask for a number, divide it by everything smaller, and if nothing divides evenly, print "prime." It worked on 7. It worked on 13. Then Jeremie, leaning over from the next laptop, had typed 1 and the program had announced, with total confidence, "prime."

"That's wrong," Jeremie said.

"It can't be wrong. It did the math."

"It did your math," said Devyn from across the table, without looking up from her screen.

Charles stared at the loop. The problem was that 1 had nothing smaller than it except, depending on how you counted, 1 itself, so nothing ever divided it, so the program declared victory. He could fix it with one line, an if statement that threw out 1 before the loop even started. But that felt like cheating. He wanted to know why 1 shouldn't count, not just that it shouldn't.

Ms. Marino wandered past, hands behind her back, the way she did when she was checking on people but pretending to consume a poster on the wall instead. She paused at his screen.

"Why is 1 not prime?" she asked. "That's your bug, by the way."

"I know it's my bug. I don't know why it's a bug. One is just one. It's not divisible by anything else, so it sounds prime to me."

"Mathematicians exclude it," she said, "so that every whole number has only one way to be written as a product of primes." Then she walked away, because she was the sort of teacher who dropped a sentence like a match and left the fire to you.

Charles sat with that. A product of primes. He grabbed the scrap paper next to his keyboard, the one covered in a vague sketch of a robot he'd drawn during announcements, and flipped it over. Twelve, he wrote. Twelve was 2 times 2 times 3. Was there another way? He tried 3 times 4, but 4 wasn't prime. He tried 2 times 6, but 6 wasn't prime either. Every road led back to the same three numbers.

Then he tried it with 1 allowed. Suddenly 12 was 2 times 2 times 3, or 1 times 2 times 2 times 3, or 1 times 1 times 2 times 2 times 3, forever. One way became infinite ways. That was the whole motive behind the rule, he realized: not that 1 had done anything wrong, just that letting it in wrecked the one-way promise for everybody else.

He typed the if statement, ran the program, and typed 1.

"Not prime," the screen said.

"Of course," Charles told it, and saved the file.

activity: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll
knowledge_domain: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll
fact: In a pick and roll, after setting the screen, the screener turns and moves toward the basket, ready for a pass from the ball handler.
story:
The gym was closed for floor repairs, so Ms. Barrett had hauled a portable hoop out to the asphalt beside the baseball diamond and told the team to practice there until further notice. Hudson was supposed to be learning to run the offense, calling plays as if he were a point guard, even though the season hadn't started yet. "You wanted this," she reminded him, tossing him the ball. "So call something."

Hudson called for a pick and roll. Sharon jogged over and planted herself beside him, arms crossed, while Clarissa, playing defense for the drill, bumped into the screen and stumbled backward. That was the moment. Hudson drove past her, looked for someone to pass to, and found nothing. Sharon was still standing where she'd set the screen, watching him, her hands on her hips. Clarissa recovered and knocked the ball away before Hudson could decide what to do with it.

"Try again," Ms. Barrett said from the bleachers by the backstop, and she said it in a way that told Hudson she'd seen exactly what had gone wrong. He wasn't sure he had. The screen had worked. Clarissa had gotten caught on it. So why had nobody been open? He thought about it while Sharon's dad arrived to pick her up early, which meant Clarissa had to play Sharon's spot and Sharon jogged off waving goodbye.

Second time through, Hudson set the screen himself this time, so he could feel the play from the other side. He planted his feet, took Clarissa's bump, and then, out of instinct more than anything, pivoted and slipped toward the basket. Clarissa's dad's car horn honked somewhere beyond the outfield fence, and in that second Hudson raised his hand and Clarissa, now with the ball, fired a bounce pass that he caught in stride and laid up off the backboard. It rattled in. He stood under the rim with the strange, bright feeling of a thing clicking into place. After setting the screen, the screener doesn't stay put. The screener turns and moves toward the basket, ready for a pass from the ball handler. Sharon had stood still because nobody had ever told her that part, and Hudson had never known to look for it because he'd only ever watched the ball.

"Once more," Ms. Barrett called, "then I'll let you commute home before dark." She was already texting Sharon's dad, asking if Sharon could come fifteen minutes early tomorrow. "She's a component you need," she said to Hudson, nodding toward the empty spot where Sharon had been standing. "That play doesn't work without her."

The next afternoon, Sharon arrived early, water bottle in hand, and found Hudson waiting at the portable hoop. "Yesterday I didn't know what I was supposed to do after I blocked Clarissa off," she admitted. "You roll," Hudson said. "Watch me once, then I'll watch you." He set the screen, felt Clarissa crowd into him, pivoted, and cut hard toward the hoop with his hand up, calling for the ball.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Psychologist Bruce Tuckman proposed in 1965 that groups go through stages called forming, storming, norming and performing.
story:
The season was only two weeks old, and Gavin's new team already had a reputation. At every practice on the dusty diamond behind the middle school, the catcher argued with the pitcher, Hazel argued with the right fielder about who should catch pop-ups, and the coach's clipboard had a dent in it from being thrown once. Gavin wanted one thing that spring: a team that actually played like a team. But every time they took the field, it fell apart in a new way.

That night he found his older sister's psychology book lying open on the couch, next to a half-eaten bag of pretzels. He only meant to move it, but a page heading caught his eye: stages that groups go through. A psychologist named Bruce Tuckman had proposed in 1965 that groups pass through stages called forming, storming, norming and performing. Gavin read it twice. Forming was when everybody was new and polite. Storming was the arguing part. His whole team was living inside a page of his sister's homework, and nobody knew it.

He couldn't wait to test the idea, so he texted Hazel, who was the only one who would actually listen. "I think the arguing is a stage, not a disaster," he wrote. "Teams are supposed to fight at first. It's called storming." He went on to explain that after the storming came norming, when a group settles into shared habits, and after that, performing, when things finally click. Hazel replied with a wall of question marks, then added, "If this is wrong, we're going to look so weird."

The next morning Gavin noticed something small. At batting practice, Hazel handed the bat to Anne without being asked, and Anne tapped the plate for her the way Hazel liked, two quick taps. Their little rituals had started to coincide, moving in step without anyone planning it. Was this norming? He watched for it all week like a bird-watcher with a checklist. When the pitcher and catcher stopped shouting and started using the same shorthand sign for a curveball, a warm feeling spread through him that had nothing to do with the sun.

The test came Saturday. In the third inning, a pop-up sailed into the gap between Hazel and the right fielder, the exact spot that had caused three screaming matches already. Gavin held his breath. Hazel called it, the right fielder peeled away, and Hazel made the catch, and then, even stranger, the right fielder jogged over and bumped her glove like they'd planned it. Two weeks ago that ball would have started a war.

Gavin ran in from shortstop, grinning. "Stage four," he said to Hazel. "Performing."

She flipped the ball to him. "Your book better be right all season," she said, "because if we storm again, I'm blaming Tuckman."

Behind them, the coach wrote something on his clipboard, carefully, without throwing it.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: In 1997, Major League Baseball retired Jackie Robinson's number 42 for every team, the first time any professional athlete was honored that way.
story:
The living room smelled like pizza, and the ceiling fan spun overhead like a small turbine, pushing warm air around because Dad refused to turn on the air conditioner during a "big game." Declan had the best seat, the corner of the couch, with Ty on the floor and Quinten wedged into the armchair with a plate balanced on his knee.

In the third inning, Quinten pointed his crust at the screen. "Every team has like forty numbers. Why has nobody ever got 42? That's the one I'd pick."

Ty shrugged. "Maybe it's bad luck."

Declan didn't think it was luck. Luck didn't remove a number from every team at once. He pulled out his phone and opened the roster page for the away team, then the home team, and scrolled. Nobody wore 42 on either side. He checked the bench players too, all the way down. Still nothing. That was a rule, not a coincidence, and rules had to be written down somewhere.

"Bet you a slice it's a rule," he said to Ty.

"You're on," Ty said.

Declan searched the number. He read for a minute, then put the phone face down on the cushion. "In 1997, Major League Baseball retired Jackie Robinson's number 42 for every team. First time any professional athlete got honored that way."

"Retired how?" Quinten asked.

"The number. Nobody on any team wears it. Ever since then."

Quinten squinted at the screen. "Wait, there's a 42 on the mound."

They all leaned in. Declan paused the picture and checked the pitcher against the roster. "That's a 2 and a 4. Number 24. My sister's TV is so small the numbers squish together."

Ty groaned and slid his plate over. Declan took the biggest slice, which was a legitimate prize, since he had won it fairly.

"You knew that already," Ty said.

"I didn't. That's why I checked the rosters before I said anything."

Quinten was quiet for a while, chewing. During the seventh-inning stretch he said, "So if Robinson wore 42, and nobody can wear it now, then every time you see a 42 somewhere, like on a shirt, that's basically a sign pointing at one guy."

"It's like his number went into hibernation," Ty said. "Asleep, but still there."

Declan shook his head. "Not asleep. Retired. A bear wakes up."

Ms. Ndlovu, who had come over to watch with the neighbors and was sitting by the door, raised her cup without looking away from the screen. "Play ball," she said.

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: On a standard 400-metre outdoor track, the 800 metres is exactly two laps, so runners plan the race as a first lap and a second lap.
story:
Alexander had been fast his whole life, which was exactly the problem. In the schoolyard, fast meant winning, because races there lasted ten seconds and ended at the fence. The park track was different. Two laps around it made eight hundred metres, and Mr. Novák had entered him in the district meet anyway, even after watching him run exactly once.

"You went out like your shoes were on fire," Bella said from the bleachers, where she was supposed to be timing him with her phone. "Then you looked like the fire won."

It was true. In his first time trial, Alexander had sprinted the opening lap so hard that by the far turn of the second one he was jogging, and Mael, who wasn't even racing, had caught up to him while eating a granola bar. Alexander had laughed then, because it was funny, but the loss had sat with him all week. Maybe being fast in short bursts wasn't the same as being fast where it counted.

On Saturday morning the three of them met at the track, and Mr. Novák marked the start line with a cone. "Two laps," he said, and walked off toward the storage shed before Alexander could ask anything else, which was his way.

Alexander stood on the line and tried to make the invisible visible. He couldn't see his own energy, couldn't measure how much a lap would cost him, but he could see the track, and the track was honest. Eight hundred metres meant the first lap and then the second lap, nothing more, and if he spent everything in the first one, the second lap would collect the debt. A plan began to germinate somewhere behind his ribs: run the first lap like a boy who had somewhere to be, not like a boy being chased. He thought of his father complaining about prices at the grocery store, how everything cost more now, and joked to Bella, "If I sprint the first lap, the second lap charges me inflation."

"Write that on a T-shirt," said Bella. "I'll buy two."

Mael ran beside him as a pacer, calling the splits. The first lap felt almost insultingly easy. "Sixty-eight seconds," Mael shouted as they crossed the line the first time, and every nerve in Alexander's legs screamed at him to go, because going was what he did. He remembered the granola bar instead. He held, he held, and then at the back stretch of lap two he let the leash out slowly, and something unexpected happened: he got faster while everyone else's plan fell apart. A runner from the other end of the park, who had blazed past them early, was suddenly shrinking ahead of him, legs gone wobbly. The boy even started pumping his arms and driving for the finish. But the finish wasn't there. That was still one lap away, and the boy didn't seem to know it.

Alexander passed him at the final bend and Bella was screaming numbers that didn't matter anymore. He crossed the line, bent double, and Mael clapped him on the back so hard he coughed.

"Two fourteen," Bella announced, holding up her phone like a trophy.

Mr. Novák came back from the shed with a clipboard, looked at the time, and said nothing, which meant everything. Later, walking home, Alexander found himself thinking about the runner who had kicked a lap too early, and about his own schoolyard self, the fastest kid at the fence. He wasn't sure which of them he'd been that first day at the park. Maybe both.

"Same time next Saturday?" Mael asked.

"Bring two granola bars," Alexander said. "One for each lap."

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: A message sent in a private chat can be screenshotted and shared by anyone who receives it, so a private message is only as private as the people who read it.
story:
The computer lab smelled like warm plastic and the lemon cleaner Ms. Sadeghi sprayed on the keyboards every Friday, no matter what. Jonathan had claimed the machine by the window because its screen didn't flicker, and he was supposed to be finishing his social studies slide about inflation, which so far consisted of one title and a picture of a sad coin. Behind him, Kye was typing fast, the way he did when he was pretending to work.

"Did you see it?" Kye whispered, sliding his chair over. He turned his monitor so only Jonathan could see. On the screen was a screenshot, clearly a screenshot because of the clock and battery icon at the top, showing a message that read: "Maelly thinks she's the boss of the group project. Someone should tell her the universe doesn't revolve around her." Below it, in the group chat for the whole class, Maelly had written: "real classy, whoever this is." The screenshot's header showed it came from a private chat, just two names.

Jonathan looked from the screenshot to Kye, then to Maelly, three rows up, arms crossed, staring at her screen like it had insulted her family. "Who sent it to the group?" he asked.

Kye shrugged, but the shrug was too fast. Jonathan thought about it. A private chat had two people in it, the sender and the receiver. The sender wouldn't share it. So the receiver had, and the receiver knew exactly who wrote it. The message was only as secret as the person who read it. "You told someone," Jonathan said quietly. "You sent it to one person to complain, and that person pasted it into the group."

"It was private," Kye hissed. "Between us. I said don't show anyone."

"You said that to the wrong guy, apparently." Jonathan turned back to his slide. The coin looked even sadder now. "If it got screenshotted, it isn't private anymore. It's as private as the person you sent it to, and that person has a big mouth."

Ms. Sadeghi walked the rows, pausing at Maelly's computer, then at Kye's. Her expression stayed neutral, which somehow made it worse. "Whoever needs to apologize," she said to the room, not to anyone in particular, "I'd coordinate that soon, before I have to." On Maelly's screen, the group project document sat open and barren except for her name at the top, all alone.

Kye stood up. His chair squeaked the length of the lab. He stopped beside Maelly's desk and said, so quietly Jonathan almost missed it, "That was about somebody else. Same name. Different Maelly."

Maelly looked at him for a long moment and typed one word into the document: "Prove it."

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: The placebo effect is when people feel better after a treatment with no active ingredient, such as a sugar pill, simply because they expect it to help.
story:
Rose sat on her bed with her phone balanced on her knees, watching the group chat light up. Forty-three messages had appeared since dinner, and all of them were about Volt Blast.

"It actually works," Fanny had written. "I drank one before practice and shaved ten whole seconds off my mile. TEN."

Jericho had replied with three lightning bolts. Mr. Quinn, who somehow ended up in every chat he wasn't supposed to be in, had typed, "Is that the one with the green label? My nephew sells it."

Rose typed slowly, then deleted, then typed again. She wanted to believe Fanny. But ten seconds was a lot, and Fanny had also once claimed a magnetic bracelet cured her hiccups. Rose had spent her leisure time that whole weekend reading about things like that, which maybe said something about her, but she didn't mind.

"Question," she posted. "Did you time yourself before the Volt Blast too?"

Fanny answered with a shrugging emoji, which was not an answer. Rose flopped back on her pillow and stared at the ceiling. She remembered the hiccup bracelet. She remembered how Fanny's hiccups had stopped exactly when she decided, really decided, the bracelet worked. Rose had borrowed the bracelet later and hiccuped for half an hour like a defective frog.

She sat up and made a plan. It was simple: she'd fill one bottle with Volt Blast and one bottle, an identical one, with water plus a drop of lemon so it looked the same. Then Jericho would drink one, run the mile, and later drink the other and run again. He wouldn't know which was which. Rose would be the only one holding the secret, and she'd hold it like a hot potato.

At the track the next morning, Jericho stretched dramatically. "I can feel it already," he announced, after drinking bottle one. "Tingling. Powerful. Like a horse."

"Run," said Rose.

He ran the mile in 7:52 and collapsed in the grass, indifferent to the ants marching over his shoe. On Sunday they came back, and he drank bottle two, the lemon water, and ran it in 7:49.

"Wait," Jericho wheezed. "Which one was the real one yesterday?"

"The real one was Sunday," Rose said. "Yesterday was lemon water."

Jericho lay in the grass, processing. "So Monday I felt like a horse because I believed I was a horse."

"There's a name for it," Rose said. "It's called the placebo effect. When people feel better after a treatment with no active ingredient, like a sugar pill, just because they expect it to help."

Fanny arrived then, holding a Volt Blast. She looked at Jericho sprawled on the track, looked at Rose's two empty bottles, and took a very long, slow sip. "I'm still buying it," she said. "It tastes like green apples."

Jericho raised one finger from the grass without lifting his head. "Get me one."

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: If clothes catch fire, the safety rule is stop, drop and roll, because running feeds the flames more oxygen.
story:
The permission slip had prescribed long pants and closed shoes for the field trip, so Joshua had swapped his sandals for sneakers before the bus pulled away from school. He sat across the aisle from Haya, who was reading the fire safety pamphlet for the third time, and behind Khaleesi, who kept turning around to ask whether they would see a real dog.
