When they arrived at the fire station, the smell hit him first, diesel and burnt toast from the kitchen, and then the trucks, enormous and polished, with hoses coiled on their sides like a giant intestine.

A firefighter led them past the trucks to a wide gray mat on the garage floor. Beside it hung a poster with big orange letters. Joshua leaned close to read it while the others crowded toward the trucks. The poster said that if your clothes catch fire, the rule is stop, drop and roll, because running feeds the flames more oxygen. He read it twice, then a third time, mouthing the words. Running feeds the flames. That was strange. His legs had always seemed like the answer to every problem, and here was a poster telling him the opposite.

"Who wants to be a volunteer?" the firefighter asked, standing on the mat. Khaleesi's hand shot up so fast it nearly hit Haya in the chin. The firefighter pointed at her, and she bounced forward, then froze halfway, her face going pink. "In front of everybody?" she said, half to herself. Joshua could see her heels already edging backward.

"You can do it," Joshua called out. "I'll go after you, so you won't be the only one rolling around on the floor looking silly." Ms. Nasser, who had been counting heads by the door, gave him a small nod, and Khaleesi's shoulders came down from around her ears.

"Stop, drop and roll," Khaleesi said to herself like a spell, and she did it, stopping dead, dropping to the mat, and rolling until the firefighter called out that the imaginary flames were out. The class cheered. Joshua went next and rolled so hard he bumped into her knee, and they both cracked up.

On the way to the smoke room, where the firefighter warned them that smoke was toxic and to stay low, Haya tugged Joshua's sleeve. "Earlier," she said, "when the alarm went off in the kitchen, that cook ran out flapping his apron. Why did he run, if running makes it worse?"

Joshua thought about the poster, and about how nobody had told the cook. "Because he panicked before he could think," he said. "The rule works only if you know it before you need it." He looked at Khaleesi, still brushing mat fuzz off her elbow, and decided he was going to teach the rule to his little brother tonight, before dinner, on the living room carpet.

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: Box breathing means breathing in for a count of four, holding for four, breathing out for four and holding for four, then repeating the pattern.
story:
Chase stood at the kitchen counter on Thursday night, staring at the permission slip for the geography bee. His name was on the list for Monday's assembly, in front of the whole school. His mom had signed the form, which meant there was no backing out. His hands were cold and his stomach hurt, even though he had not eaten since lunch. He assumed the stomach ache was from the cafeteria pizza, until he noticed his shoulders were up near his ears and he had been grinding his teeth since dinner.

He texted Winter, who had done the spelling bee last year and had not fainted, which made her the expert as far as he was concerned. She called him back right away.

"Did you eat something weird?" she asked.

"Pizza. But my hands are cold too, and I keep grinding my teeth."

"That's not pizza. That's stress. Your body does stuff before your brain catches on." She paused. "Remember Arizona at the science fair? She was tracing a square on the desk with her finger before her turn, over and over. It's called box breathing. Four counts in, four counts holding, four counts out, four counts holding, then you just repeat the pattern. The square she drew had one side for each count of four."

"So I breathe in for four seconds, then hold for four, then out for four, then hold again?"

"That's the whole thing. You can draw the square on your leg if your hands shake, like hers did."

He hung up and tried it at the counter, drawing a square on the countertop with one finger. In for four counts along the top edge. Hold for four down the side. Out for four along the bottom. Hold for four going back up. After five squares his shoulders had come down off his ears. His hands were still cool but not ice. He kept going until the microwave clock changed by two minutes.

The stomach ache faded, which proved Winter's point. His body had been running an alarm with no fire. The irony was that the thing he feared, standing up Monday, was being ruined in advance by the fear itself, in his own kitchen, three days early.

There was still the night problem. Every time a bee came up, he lay awake replaying the time in fourth grade when he blanked on the word "isthmus" and a kid in the second row had laughed for a solid minute. He decided to test an idea: what if sleep needed a pattern too, the same way breathing did? He made a routine and wrote it on the fridge whiteboard. Phone on the counter at nine, not in his room. Same three stretches. Lights out at nine thirty, every night, bee or no bee, starting tonight.

Friday he slept through the night for the first time all week. Saturday he did the routine again and added the square breathing while lying in bed, finger tracing the shape on the blanket. Sunday night he caught his shoulders climbing toward his ears while he thought about the auditorium, so he ran ten slow squares until his jaw unclenched.

Monday morning, before the bus, he practiced one last time at the counter. His mom watched him draw the invisible square on the countertop and pour his cereal with a steady hand.

"Feeling ready?" she asked.

"Approximately," he said, and traced the first edge. "In, two, three, four."

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: In Excel, a 'bar chart' has horizontal bars and a 'column chart' has vertical bars, although both compare amounts across categories.
story:
Grandpa's laptop had a sticky E key, so every time Scarlett typed "SUM," it came out "SUME" and the formula sulked at her in a little green triangle. She pried the key up with a butter knife, blew a crumb out from under it, and tried again. This time the cell at the bottom of her Allowance column flipped to a number: 46.75. She had actually done it. She had made a formula that added a whole column by itself.

"Whoa," said Jeremi, leaning over her shoulder at the kitchen table. "It did math without you."

"It did math without me," Scarlett agreed, and did a small drumroll on the table. Grandpa's plan was simple. He kept a jar of coins, and he'd promised to accelerate the rewards if Scarlett tracked his mysterious candy spending for one week and showed him a chart by Sunday dinner. Sunday dinner was in ninety minutes.

Aryana arrived with the coin jar hugged against her chest like a baby. "I counted it last night while you two were fighting with the E key. Grandpa spends the most on licorice. I want him to see that in giant letters."

"Bars," Scarlett said. "Not letters, bars." She selected her candy data, clicked Insert, chose the first chart that looked right, and hit Enter.

The chart appeared sideways. The licorice bar lay flat along the bottom like it had fallen asleep. Aryana gasped as if the computer had committed a crime. "It's broken. Fix it before Grandpa sees. He'll blame me, I'm holding the jar."

Scarlett frowned at the screen. Every chart she'd ever imagined had bars standing up. She scrolled through the chart options and found two names sitting side by side: column chart and bar chart. She picked the column chart instead, and the bars straightened up into tall towers, licorice towering over everything. "It wasn't broken," she said slowly. "I picked the sideways one. A bar chart has horizontal bars. A column chart has vertical ones."

"So a bar chart isn't even a column chart," Jeremi said, poking the screen. "That's like a hot dog not being a sandwich."

"It's exactly like that," Scarlett said. She added a title, and because the anonymous culprit behind the missing chocolate coins deserved blame, she labeled the licorice bar "GRANDPA'S DOWNFALL."

At dinner, Grandpa held the laptop at arm's length, squinted, then laughed so hard he nearly dropped his fork. "Licorice, my downfall indeed." He slid three chocolate coins across the table to Aryana, who caught them midair.

"Your hierarchy of candy is officially exposed," Scarlett told him, tapping the tall licorice tower one last time.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Fire-safety guidance says to put out a campfire by drowning it with water, stirring the ashes, and drowning it again until everything is cool to the touch.
story:
Audrey's family was supposed to leave the campsite by nine, but the fire pit was still warm. Her dad had dumped a bucket of water on it an hour ago, and the ashes had stopped smoking, but when Audrey waved her hand over them, she could still feel heat, like a radiator in spring. "It's fine," her dad said, loading the cooler into the trunk. "Water beats fire. That's the whole fight."

Audrey wasn't so sure. She crouched beside the stone ring and studied the ashes. The top layer was grey and dead-looking, but a piece of charred log near the edge had a dull orange line along its underside, like a secret. She deduced that the water had only drowned the surface, and that the hot part was hiding underneath, where the water hadn't reached. If that was true, then pouring more water on top would do the same thing twice: cool the lid, leave the stove.

She found Emmie and Gerald at the picnic table, scraping maple syrup off their fingers with napkins. "I need your bucket," Audrey said. Gerald groaned. "The fire's out. I saw steam. Steam means out." "Steam means the water's out," Audrey said. "The fire might still be under there." Emmie, whose goal in life was a scholarship to a science camp where she could set things on fire legally, stood up so fast she knocked over the syrup bottle.

Audrey filled the bucket at the pump and dumped it on the ashes. Then she took a stick and stirred, digging down through the grey layer into black chunks underneath. A puff of steam hissed up, smelling like wet charcoal and old hot dogs. "Told you," she said. She poured on a second bucket, drowning everything until the water pooled in the low spots of the pit, dark and gritty. She kept her voice neutral when she said "touch test" to herself, because part of her wanted to brag.

The back of her hand hovered over the ashes. Warm. She stirred again, knocked the chunks apart, and dumped a third bucket. This time, when she touched the ashes with her fingertips, they were cool and clammy, like wet sidewalk. No orange lines anywhere. Gerald poked a black chunk with his shoe. "Okay," he said. "That was actually kind of great."

Her dad leaned against the car, arms crossed, watching. "Where'd you learn that?" "Nobody told me," Audrey said. "The middle was still hot, so the middle needed the water." She rinsed her hands at the pump, dried them on her shorts, and picked up the last bag of marshmallows. "You owe me the window seat," she said.

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: Sprinting the first lap faster than a pace you can hold uses up quick anaerobic energy early, so the runner usually slows sharply on the second lap.
story:
The first time Lea ran the eight hundred metres in gym class, she sprinted off the line like the ground behind her was on fire. She led the whole first lap, her ponytail streaming, and Landen shouted, "You're winning!" Then somewhere on the second lap her legs turned to noodles, and five people passed her before the finish. She ended up sixth and spent the walk back to the changeroom trying not to cry.

Mr. Nakamura handed out strips of paper the next day. "Time trials on Friday," he said. "Eight hundred metres again." Lea stared at hers. Sixth place she could live with. Sixth place while feeling like a melting snowman, she could not.

At lunch she watched Landen eat his sandwich, and an idea began to bother her. "Landen, on Monday, when I blew up, where was I at the start of the second lap?" Landen thought with his mouth full. "First. Easily first. Then Yanis passed you by the water fountain, and after that it was like a parade going by you." A parade. Lea drew two circles in her notebook. She had gone out fast, faster than a pace she could hold, and she had slowed sharply on the second lap. Every runner who had passed her had looked comfortable on lap one, like they were saving something. She wrote underneath: fast first lap, slow second lap. Test: even laps.

Wednesday after school she tried it on the track alone, with Yanis holding the stopwatch. "Don't fly out like a startled pigeon," Yanis advised. "Noted," said Lea. She counted her steps, held back when her legs begged to zoom, and crossed the first lap slower than she ever had on purpose. It felt almost embarrassing. Then, on the second lap, she found she still had something left, and she sped up instead of slowing down. Her two laps were nearly the same time. Yanis showed her the watch and raised both eyebrows. "Huh."

Friday, Mr. Nakamura blew his whistle. Lea stuck to her plan even when a girl from Mr. Nakamura's other class tore away at the start, arms pumping, clearly the fastest thing on the track. Lea ran her own race. Sure enough, on the back curve of the second lap, the fast girl began to fade, her steps shortening, and one by one the parade went by her: Lea included, right on the final straight.

Lea finished second, breathing hard, her shirt starting to perspire in the cool air, and Landen wrapped her in a hug that smelled like peanut butter. "You passed that girl like she was a mailbox!" Yanis jogged over, grinning, and said, "You looked durable out there. Like a good pair of boots." Lea laughed. She had felt many things during that race, but boot-like was new. "That girl who faded," she said, pointing to the leader-turned-mailbox, who was now bent over, hands on her knees. Yanis nodded. "Happens every year. Somebody always burns it all on lap one." Lea thought about walking over to tell the girl what she had figured out, because she knew exactly how that felt. Empathy, her mom called it. She grabbed her water bottle, trotted across the infield, and said, "Hey. Want to see something I wrote in my notebook?"

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: In February 2015 a photo of a dress went viral because some people saw it as blue and black and others as white and gold; the real dress was blue and black.
story:
The argument started before homeroom, when Alexi held a phone screen up to Mila's face and demanded, "Tell me this dress is white and gold."

Mila looked. The photo showed a lacy dress on a hanger, shot in bad lighting. "It's blue and black," she said. "Obviously."

Alexi made a sound like a kettle. Leonardo leaned over from the next desk and studied the same screen. "White and gold," he said. "Sorry, Alexi, I'm on your side, but that thing is white and gold."

"You're agreeing with me by disagreeing with her," Alexi said. "That counts as winning."

By lunch, the whole cafeteria had picked sides. Mr. Lombardi, who monitored lunch duty, walked past the table, glanced at the phone, and said, "Blue and black," then kept walking with his tray of meatloaf as though nothing unusual had occurred. Mila's table erupted. Someone at the far table claimed white and gold, and a seventh grader stood on a chair to conduct a poll by shouting.

Mila kept thinking about a Saturday three weeks earlier, when her cousin had gotten a mild concussion at the skate park and spent the evening in a dim room. At one point her aunt held up a translucent curtain and asked what color the light through it looked like, testing her cousin's eyes, and her cousin had said one thing and her aunt had sworn the light was another. The doctors had shrugged. Brains, they said, report things differently sometimes. Mila had filed it away as a weird family story. Now she wasn't so sure it was just a family thing.

She had a theory, and she wanted to test it. If two people saw the same photo differently, then the same two people should still agree on something ordinary, like a marker. She borrowed a blue marker from Mr. Lombardi's desk on the way to fifth period, marched it back to Alexi, and held it beside the phone. "What color is this?"

"Blue," Alexi said. "Duh."

"And the dress?"

"White and gold. Next to a blue marker. Which is insane, and yet."

Leonardo tried it too and got the same split, marker blue, dress gold. Mila revised her first idea, which had been that Alexi was simply wrong on purpose to be annoying. That theory was dead. Something stranger was going on, and it clearly wasn't about eyesight in any ordinary way.

After school she looked it up in the computer lab. The photo had gone viral in February 2015, and the whole internet had split exactly the same way, some people seeing blue and black, others white and gold. She scrolled further and found the ending of the mystery: the real dress was blue and black.

She ran the search result out to the courtyard, where Alexi and Leonardo were waiting by the bike racks. "Okay," she said, holding up the screen. "The actual dress is blue and black. It's a real dress, in a store."

Alexi stared at the screen. "Then my eyes are lying to me."

"Mine too," said Leonardo, "which is somehow worse."

Mila grinned and put the phone away. "Tomorrow I'm bringing a printout. Let's find out what Mr. Lombardi's meatloaf really is."

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: Two players can have the same average while one is steady and the other swings between great and terrible games, since an average hides how spread out the results are.
story:
The bus rattled past the hardware store where workers were going to renovate the old front, and Daniel barely glanced at it. He had the sign-up sheet for Saturday's three-on-three basketball tournament folded in his pocket, and he was down to the last roster spot. Samy slid into the seat beside him, backpack first.

"Tell me you picked someone," Samy said.

"Not yet. It's between Nolan and Marcus from Ms. Santos's class. I wrote down every game they played at lunch this week." Daniel unfolded a page of pencil marks. "Nolan scored eight, nine, eight, nine, ten. Marcus scored zero, zero, eighteen, eighteen, eight. Both of them add up to forty-four points, so their average is the same."

Samy leaned over to read the page. "Then flip a coin."

"It's not the same," Daniel said. "Watch." He covered Marcus's scores with his thumb, then uncovered them one at a time. "Nolan gives you eight or nine every single game. Marcus gives you nothing half the time. If he has a bad game Saturday, we're playing two against three." He tried it again with the numbers, moving them around, and the pattern stayed put. Same average, but the games underneath it looked nothing alike.

"So you're saying a coin flip is wrong," Samy said.

"I'm saying the average can't tell them apart. Something else has to." Daniel tapped the pencil against the seat back. The bus stopped, and a group of sixth graders pushed past, arguing about a video game ranking. Daniel listened to one of them insist he was ranked higher even though his percentage of wins was lower, because he had played twice as many matches. Numbers squashing a whole season into one line, Daniel thought, just like his lunch scores.

At the next stop Marcus got on. He dropped into the seat across the aisle, saw the sheet, and raised his eyebrows. "You picking me or Nolan?"

"Neither of you yet," Daniel said. "You both average the same points. But Nolan's steady, and you're either brilliant or invisible, and I can't tell which one shows up on a given day."

Marcus grinned. "Take Nolan then. Even I don't know which one shows up."

Daniel circled Nolan's name. "Tell you what, though. If we're losing at halftime, you're my first substitution."

"Deal," said Marcus, and held out his fist over the aisle.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: One of the first written guides to online manners, 'Netiquette Guidelines', was published in 1995 as a document called RFC 1855.
story:
Grace's phone buzzed against her math homework, and she almost knocked over her water glass grabbing it. The new class group chat, the one Ms. Reyes had approved on Friday, already had sixty-two messages, and Grace had left it alone for twenty minutes. Twenty minutes. She scrolled up through a wall of capital letters. SOMEONE TOOK MY SPOT IN THE LAB LINE, Myriam had written, and then Imran had answered in capitals too, and then three other kids she barely knew had piled on, each message louder than the last, as if shouting were contagious, like a virus spreading through the chat one ALL CAPS message at a time.

Ms. Reyes had put Grace in charge of the chat's rules, which had seemed like an honor at the time and now felt like being handed a leaking bucket. Grace sat cross-legged on her bed, chewing the end of her pencil. She knew the rules for talking to people face to face. You didn't shout at Myriam in the hallway, and you didn't announce embarrassing things in front of the whole class. But online, everyone seemed to forget. And the worst part was that Grace couldn't tell what was a joke and what was real anger. Myriam's message could be either. That was the hidden problem, and Grace couldn't see it directly, only its shadow: sixty-two messages, escalating.

She typed a test. "Hey, Myriam, were you actually mad or just joking?" The reply came fast. "joking obviously." Then, a second later: "everyone thought i was mad though." Grace sat very still. That was it. Myriam's tone had come across wrong because caps and no punctuation and no face, all the things that normally told you how someone felt, were missing. In private, between the two of them in direct messages, Myriam wrote calmly, lowercase, patient. In the public chat, she performed for an audience. Same girl, two different voices.

Grace needed rules, but she wanted them to be official, not just made up by her. "Did anyone ever actually write down manners for the internet?" she muttered, and pulled her laptop over. She searched, expecting nothing, expecting that online manners were as extinct as the dinosaurs. Instead a page came up that made her sit up straight. One of the first written guides to online manners, called "Netiquette Guidelines," had been published in 1995 as a document called RFC 1855. She read it twice. 1995. Before she was born, before smartphones, and people had already noticed the exact problem in her chat: it was hard to read tone, and shouting in capitals made things worse.

At school the next morning, Ms. Reyes gave the class five minutes of chat business before the lab. Grace stood up, her ears radiating heat, and held her phone like a tiny podium.

"Turns out this isn't a new problem," she said. "There's a real guide. It's called the 'Netiquette Guidelines,' and it was published in 1995 as a document called RFC 1855." A couple of kids snickered at the number. "Before any of us existed," Grace said, "and it says don't type in all caps, because people can't tell if you're joking or yelling." She paused. "So I made us a rule. Public chat, normal letters only. Jokes get an emoji or a 'jk' so nobody panics."

Imran raised his hand slowly. "So yesterday, when Myriam wrote in caps, and I wrote back in caps, we were both yelling at nothing?" Myriam spun around in her seat.

"We were fighting a war that didn't exist," she said, and started laughing, and Imran laughed too, and Grace watched sixty-two messages of pretend anger collapse into three seconds of real giggling. Then she pulled up the chat and pinned the new rules to the top.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: A pet microchip has no GPS and cannot track where an animal is; it only gives its ID number when a scanner is held close.
story:
The carrier wobbled in Evan's hands all the way from the car to his bedroom, and inside it the kitten, Nutmeg, yowled like a tiny storm. "Welcome home," Evan whispered, setting the carrier on his bed. His dad had signed the papers at the shelter an hour ago, and the woman at the desk had said the words Evan couldn't stop thinking about: "She's microchipped."

Kenzi and Drew showed up before he'd even latched the carrier door. "You said it has a chip," Drew said, leaning over Nutmeg, who flattened her ears and backed into the corner. "So where's the map?"

Evan pulled out his phone, grinning. That was the plan. He'd imagined it on the drive home: a little orange dot, Nutmeg's dot, moving across a map of the neighborhood whenever she squeezed through a fence or vanished under the porch. He typed "microchip tracker" into the search bar and waited, thumb bouncing against his knee.

Nothing came up that looked like a map. The results were pages about scanners and ID numbers, and the more he scrolled, the more his grin went brittle around the edges. Kenzi took the phone, read for a minute, and handed it back. "It says a microchip has no GPS and can't track where an animal is," she said slowly. "It only gives its ID number when a scanner is held close."

"Close like how close?" Drew asked.

"Like at the vet's office," Kenzi said.

Evan stared at the phone, then at the kitten. "So if Nutmeg runs away, the chip won't tell me where she is. It just tells whoever finds her who she is." He thought about the dots on the map he'd imagined, all those invisible little signals he'd assumed were flying around, and felt almost embarrassed. He had wanted so badly to see that map that he'd read the word "chip" and made up the rest. That was a bias, he decided, toward good news.

"So we test it," Drew said, because Drew always wanted to test things.

Nutmeg chose that moment to bolt. She shot out of the carrier, ricocheted off a pillow, and vanished somewhere behind Evan's desk. Evan lunged, dropped the phone, and crouched with his cheek on the carpet, peering into the dark gap where two amber eyes blinked back at him.

He held the phone out flat on the floor, screen glowing. "Nope," he reported. "No dot. I have no idea where she is except that I can see her."

Kenzi laughed and grabbed the half-full carrier. "Then we catch her the old way. Drew, get the string."

Nutmeg's tail twitched once at the edge of the shadow.

activity: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
knowledge_domain: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
fact: Jewish views of the afterlife vary widely: Orthodox Judaism holds to a future resurrection of the dead, while Reform Judaism puts more weight on how people live now.
story:
The gate of Hillcrest Cemetery was old enough that it squeaked in two different notes, and George noticed that the low note came when he pushed it slowly and the high note when he pushed it fast. Everything had a mechanism, his dad always said, even squeaky gates. George had come with his class on a foggy Saturday morning because Mr. Jung, who took care of the grounds, had invited the school to see the historic Jewish section before it got restored.

"You two are coming with me," Mr. Jung said to Lane and Annabel, because the teacher wanted the Jewish kids to help read the worn headstones. "You're cousins, right? You can translate faster than I can."

"Faster than each other, anyway," Annabel said in her assertive way, the way she talked in class when she was sure she was right and wanted everyone to know it. "Lane's from the other side of town. Different synagogue."

They walked between rows of stones with Hebrew letters softened by a hundred winters. George trailed behind them, thinking about something he had wondered for weeks. His grandmother had died in the spring, and he had overheard adults at the funeral saying things about where she was now, and the strange part was that they didn't all say the same thing. He had a hypothesis, which was a word he'd learned in science class: maybe the differences weren't random. Maybe they followed a pattern, and he could find it by asking the same question twice.

"So," he said, keeping his voice casual, "what happens after you die? Like, in your religion." He asked Lane first.

Lane wiped lichen off a stone with his sleeve. "The dead will be resurrected. That's what we believe. Someday, at the end, they rise up again."

Annabel frowned at him like he'd said something backwards. "That's not what we say at our synagogue. We focus on this life. What matters is what you do now, how you live."

They stared at each other. "We're both Jewish," Lane said. "How can we believe two different things?"

George's pulse did a small jump, the way it did when an experiment worked. Here was his evidence. Lane's family was Orthodox, Annabel's was Reform, and the two answers split exactly along that line, the way iron filings line up with a magnet. He could deduce the rule from only two data points, which was thin, but it was a start. He wanted more.

"Mr. Jung," he called, "do you know the families buried here? Which were which?"

Mr. Jung ran his thumb along a carved name. "Some of these stones have hands carved on them, some have stars, some have nothing at all. Different congregations, different centuries. Even among the Jewish families here, the old records show they didn't all describe the world to come the same way." He handed George a clipboard. "Write down the symbols, row by row. Let's see what we find."

So George counted. Hands, forty-one. Plain stones, sixty-three. Stars, nine. He graphed it in his notebook, and the numbers clustered in sections, as if whole groups had sorted themselves by belief before they ever got buried. He was still puzzling over what the mechanism could be, whether people chose neighbors who shared their hopes, when Lane pointed at a small stone near the fence.

"That one has both," Lane said. "Hands and a star. Same grave."

"Two families?" Annabel guessed.

"Or one family that split," George said slowly, "like you two."

Annabel opened her mouth, closed it, and then started to laugh. "Okay, that's actually possible. Lane, our great-great-something might be right there."

Lane got down on his knees in the wet grass to read the half-vanished name. "Gershon," he said. "Gershon, son of Leah."

"Then we're related to a mystery," Annabel said, kneeling beside him.

activity: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
knowledge_domain: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
fact: In Stephen Toulmin's model of argument, the claim is the point being argued, and the grounds or data are the evidence given to support it.
story:
Brooklyn slapped three sticky notes onto the lunch table like she was dealing cards. "Topic is banning homework. I say we win this thing."

Wilson leaned over his tray. "Your first note just says homework is bad."

"That's my claim," Brooklyn said. "The point being argued. Write it down, Wilson, that's your whole job."

Greta pulled the note toward her. "And the other two?"

"Reasons homework is bad." Brooklyn grinned. "Reason one, it ruins weekends. Reason two, it turns kids into zombies."

Mr. Rao, who ran the debate club and apparently had radar for sticky notes, appeared behind them with his coffee. "Zombies," he repeated. "Interesting. In the Toulmin model, a claim is the point being argued, and the grounds, sometimes called the data, are the evidence that supports it. So." He pointed at each note in turn. "Claim. Opinion. Opinion." Then he walked off toward the vending machine, humming.

Brooklyn stared at the notes. Last year she had done this exact thing, she remembered, standing up in Ms. Park's class to declare that school lunches were a crime, and Tomas Reyes had simply asked, "Says who?" She'd had nothing. She had sat down next to the humid radiator and felt her face burn hotter than it.

"Not again," she muttered. "Wilson, we need data. Real data."

Wilson raised his hand like they were still in class. "My cousin had a double ear infection last month and still had to do a math packet. Is that data?"

"It's a story," Greta said. "One cousin is not a pattern."

But Brooklyn was already flipping her notebook open. Here was her idea, and it was so simple she felt silly for not testing it sooner: she would put every sentence they planned to say through one question, "where's the evidence," and anything that died there got cut. "Homework ruins weekends," she read aloud. "Evidence?"

Wilson shrugged. "We could count how many kids did homework last Saturday."

Greta grabbed a fresh sheet of paper. "We survey the whole grade at lunch. Two questions. Then we have numbers."

They spent the next lunch stationed outside the cafeteria, sweating in the humid hallway air, collecting answers from anyone who would stop. Twenty-eight kids, and nineteen of them had done at least an hour of schoolwork on Saturday. Two claimed they were zombies already, which Greta crossed out.

"So the claim is homework takes weekend time," Brooklyn said slowly, writing, "and the grounds are nineteen out of twenty-eight students. And then we need the part that connects them. Why do those numbers prove the claim?"

Wilson squinted at her page. "Because an hour on Saturday is an hour not spent riding bikes?"

"Elaborate," Brooklyn said, tapping her pen.

"Because... time is finite? Like, you can't get it back?" Wilson threw his hands up. "I don't know, it sounds smarter when I say it out loud."

"It sounds like a link," Brooklyn said. "Claim, grounds, link. Every point gets all three or it goes in the trash." She held up the zombie note, considered it with great ceremony, and dropped it into the garbage can by the door.

At Thursday's practice debate, the other team stood up and announced that homework built character, that homework taught discipline, that homework was a sacred tradition. Brooklyn stood, pointed at their first speaker, and asked, "Where's your evidence?"

Nobody said anything for a full five seconds. Mr. Rao smiled into his coffee.

Brooklyn leaned toward the microphone. "Nineteen out of twenty-eight students, folks. Check the sticky notes."

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: Loaded words carry strong feelings beyond their plain meaning, so calling the same crowd "protesters" or "rioters" can push readers toward opposite opinions.
story:
Aaron spread the two newspapers across the coffee table in his living room, one on top of the other like an archaeologist about to excavate a buried city. Dexter flopped onto the couch beside him with his laptop. "Same rally, same day, same park," Aaron said, tapping the first headline. "Read this one out loud."

"'Thousands of protesters filled the square demanding cleaner water,'" Dexter read. Then he slid the laptop over. "And this site says, 'Rioters clashed with police downtown.'" He frowned at both. "Okay, that's weird. It feels like two different things happened."

Aaron remembered their teacher saying the class project had to compare how the same story got told in different places, and he had shrugged at the time. Now the shrug felt brittle, like it might crack, because the difference was sitting right in front of him. He read both headlines again, slower. Thousands of peaceful people versus a violent mob. Same crowd. The only thing that had changed was the word.

"Try this," Aaron said. He copied both headlines into a blank document and swapped the words. "'Rioters filled the square demanding cleaner water.' Ugh. I picture broken windows, and they were just holding signs." Dexter typed fast, then leaned back. "'Protesters clashed with police.' That almost sounds reasonable, like a disagreement." He looked at Aaron. "So the word does it. The word pushes you." Aaron nodded. "My dad says they're loaded words. They carry a feeling, like a backpack full of rocks. 'Protesters' makes you feel a little empathy for them. 'Rioters' makes you want them stopped."

Then Dexter spun the laptop toward the TV, where a commercial was playing. A famous basketball player grinned at the camera and said he only drank a certain sports drink, and everyone was drinking it, millions of fans, everybody. "See, that's the other stuff," Dexter said, counting on his fingers. "Celebrity guy says buy it, and then they tell you the whole world already did. My little sister fell for that last week with some sneaker thing." Aaron laughed. "They're stacking the tricks. Famous person plus 'everyone has it' plus, I bet, some loaded word in there." He grabbed a pen and circled "revolutionary" in the ad's caption on the screen. "That's a loaded word too."

They worked until the room went dim, marking every technique they could find in a pile of ads and headlines. Aaron's list had three columns now: bandwagon, testimonial, loaded words. Outside, a leaf blower roared, and their neighbor Mr. Mendoza waved from his porch. Dexter snapped the laptop shut. "So for our project, we show people the same crowd with two different words and see if they fall for it?" Aaron was already pulling out his phone to record. "We'll ask five people. Watch this."

He hit record and held up the first headline. "Read this and tell me what kind of people they are."
